modalities.name: Long Settle Imagery
modalities.tagline: Deep calm first, then one slow scene of being cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Long Settle Imagery is a new, untested idea that pushes ideal parent imagery (picturing yourself as a child cared for by invented, ideal parents) further toward calm and absorption than the original method. A trained therapist spends most of a long session helping you settle deeply, then guides one slow, unchanging scene of being cared for, instead of exploring or talking with different sides of yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that care might sink in more fully when you are deeply settled and simply receiving, so the session spends its time on settling and receiving rather than on talking or exploring.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 90-minute session, the therapist guides about 40 minutes of slow settling through the breath, a body scan and a gradual quieting of thought. Then comes a single, carefully paced scene in which ideal parents protect, soothe and delight in the child you imagine being, followed by a slow return and a short talk about what stayed with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with lasting insecurity in close relationships who find that talk-heavy therapy keeps them in their heads, and who settle well with guided relaxation.
modalities.cautions: Deep calm can lower defenses, so painful memories of your real childhood may surface, and long relaxation can blur imagination and memory; it should only be done with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps the scene clearly imagined. People prone to dissociation should avoid long relaxation inductions, and it is not a replacement for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Long Settle Imagery. A therapist spends most of the session helping you sink into deep calm, then guides one slow scene of being cared for by imagined ideal parents. For people whose minds stay busy in talk therapy. Untested, so go gently.

modalities.name: The Wordless Cradle
modalities.tagline: Imagined care from the time before you had words.
modalities.whatItIs: The Wordless Cradle is a proposed practice that takes ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, back to the earliest part of life, before language. Instead of scenes with conversations, you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked, fed and kept warm by ideal parents, and you mostly notice how that care feels in your body.
modalities.coreIdea: The first lessons about whether care can be relied on are learned before words, so this practice works with wordless, bodily images of being held rather than with talk, agendas or structured steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying or reclining under a blanket, you follow a therapist's slow, sparse descriptions of being held close, rocked and warmed, with long quiet pauses in between. There is no goal to reach and little talking; at the end you describe in a few words what you felt, and the therapist checks how settled you are before you leave.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who sense that their insecurity runs deeper than any memory and who find that words get in the way of feeling cared for.
modalities.cautions: Imagining infancy can bring up strong, hard-to-name feelings of longing or grief and can feel very exposing, so it belongs only with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps the pace slow. It must never be used to 'recover' memories from infancy, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea: The Wordless Cradle. With a trained therapist you imagine being a baby who is held, rocked and kept warm by ideal parents, with almost no talking. For adults whose insecurity feels older than words. Untested, and only with a trauma-aware guide.

modalities.name: One Age at a Time
modalities.tagline: Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood.
modalities.whatItIs: One Age at a Time is a new, untested idea that turns ideal parent imagery into a planned journey through childhood, from toddler to teenager. Each block of sessions imagines ideal parents meeting the needs of one age, such as a five-year-old's fears at night or a teenager's need for both freedom and limits.
modalities.coreIdea: Children need different kinds of care at different ages, so this practice offers imagined care stage by stage, rather than as one general scene, and moves on only when an age feels settled.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a trained therapist first choose about six ages to visit, from around two to sixteen. Over several weekly sessions per age, the therapist guides scenes of ideal parents caring for you at that age, and you rate how settled it feels before moving on to the next.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who notice that their struggles in relationships feel tied to particular stages, such as early school years or adolescence, and who like a clear long-term plan.
modalities.cautions: Moving through the years can stir up memories of what really happened at each age, so this needs a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps imagined scenes separate from memories. It is long-term work with no evidence behind it yet, and it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: One Age at a Time. Ideal parent imagery as a planned journey through childhood, one age per block of sessions, from toddler to teen, each with the care that age needed. For adults who feel stuck at one stage. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Tucked In Imagery
modalities.tagline: Comfort only: an imagined bedtime with parents who stay.
modalities.whatItIs: Tucked In Imagery is a gentle, speculative variation on ideal parent imagery that stays entirely on soothing, with no searching for what hurts or why. Each session imagines one ordinary bedtime: ideal parents settling the child you picture being, staying close and leaving a light on, until the scene ends in safe, sleepy calm.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people may need to feel soothed many times before they can safely look at anything painful, so this practice offers comfort only and never goes digging.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie or recline in a dim, quiet room while the therapist guides a 20-minute bedtime scene: a bath, a story, a tucking in, and parents who stay until you feel drowsy. Afterwards you rest for a few minutes, sit up slowly and talk briefly about how calm you feel, rather than about the past.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel on edge most of the time, find bedtime or being alone at night hard, and want a gentle way in before any deeper work.
modalities.cautions: Even soothing scenes can awaken grief for the care you missed, so it still needs a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work, and any other care you receive should continue. Deep relaxation can leave some people drowsy or spacey, so take a few minutes before driving.
modalities.tweet: What if therapy began with being tucked in? Tucked In Imagery is a new idea: a therapist guides a calm bedtime scene where ideal parents settle the child you picture being, with no digging into the past. For people who rarely feel safe enough to rest.

modalities.name: The Letter Drawer
modalities.tagline: Care from imagined ideal parents, written down and kept.
modalities.whatItIs: The Letter Drawer moves ideal parent work, the practice of experiencing care from invented ideal parents, entirely into words, with no body work at all. With a therapist, you compose letters in the voice of imagined ideal parents, written to the child you were, read them aloud in session and keep them together to reread.
modalities.coreIdea: Words can be kept, reread and carried around, so care written down in a clear, steady voice might become a lasting reminder in a way that a passing scene cannot.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each weekly session, the therapist helps you draft one short letter in the ideal parents' voice, answering a specific need such as being comforted after a bad day at school. You read it aloud slowly, notice which lines land, and add it to a folder or box that you reread between sessions, with the therapist's guidance on when to pause.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel more at home with words than with body sensations or visualizing, and who want something they can hold on to between sessions.
modalities.cautions: Writing to your younger self can bring up grief or anger about your real childhood, so this should be done with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work, and the letters should be clearly marked as imagined rather than as a version of what happened. It is an untested idea and not a replacement for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: New idea: The Letter Drawer. With a therapist, you write short letters from imagined ideal parents to the child you were, read them aloud and keep them to reread. Care you can hold, for people who think in words. Untested and best done with support.

modalities.name: Someone Steps In
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who act firmly to keep the child safe.
modalities.whatItIs: Someone Steps In is an experimental take on ideal parent imagery, in which you picture yourself as a child cared for by invented ideal parents, that focuses on one quality above all: protection. Where gentler methods wait to see what comes, the therapist plans each scene so that imagined ideal parents act firmly on the child's behalf, standing between the child and harm, saying no to unfair treatment and making things safe.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling protected may need to be experienced as decisive action by someone strong, so every scene is planned to end with that person having clearly stepped in.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the imagery begins, you and the therapist agree on a kind of situation where you felt unprotected as a child, such as being teased or left out, without going over details, and invent a scene (not a memory) in which ideal parents arrive and take charge. The therapist then guides that scene slowly, step by step, and you notice the moment it starts to feel safe.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up feeling that no one would stand up for them, and who still freeze, over-apologize or fight alone when someone is unfair to them.
modalities.cautions: Scenes about being unprotected sit close to real hurts, so this is only for work with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care who keeps the scenes invented rather than replayed memories. It is untested and should not replace well-tested treatments for trauma.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Someone Steps In. Guided imagery where invented ideal parents act firmly to protect the child you once were, stepping between you and harm. For adults who grew up feeling no one would stand up for them. Untested; a job for a trauma-trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Five Gifts Course
modalities.tagline: One structured module for each quality of secure care.
modalities.whatItIs: The Five Gifts Course would turn ideal parent imagery into a structured program with one module for each quality of secure care: protection, soothing, being understood, encouragement to explore, and delight. Each module has set scenes, home recordings and simple ratings, so progress is planned and visible rather than left to unfold on its own.
modalities.coreIdea: Building each quality of felt security on purpose, one at a time, might make the work easier to follow and to track than open-ended sessions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 15 weekly sessions, three per quality, a trained therapist guides a scripted scene focused on that module's gift and gives you a short recording to use at home. At the start and end of each module you rate statements such as 'I can be comforted' from 0 to 10, and the therapist slows the pace if a module stirs up too much.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with insecure attachment who like clear structure, measurable steps and knowing what comes next.
modalities.cautions: Set steps can feel pressured when old pain surfaces, so the therapist, who should be trained in attachment and trauma work, must be free to slow down or stop. The ratings are a guide rather than proof, and the course is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who like structure: The Five Gifts Course. Ideal parent imagery as a planned program, one module each for protection, soothing, being understood, encouragement and delight, with simple ratings to track how it feels. Untested, therapist-led.

modalities.name: Twin Guide Intensive
modalities.tagline: A few planned days of imagery, with two practitioners present.
modalities.whatItIs: Twin Guide Intensive is an untested concept that runs ideal parent imagery as a concentrated block of sessions over a few days, with every minute planned. Two trained practitioners work together: one voices and guides the imagery while the other watches your breathing and posture, tracks your comfort and calls pauses.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentrated, carefully planned time with imagined care might build momentum that weekly sessions lose between visits, and a second practitioner makes that intensity safer to hold.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over three to five days you have two or three planned sessions a day, each with a short settling, a scripted scene and a structured debrief, plus rest breaks and meals at set times. Both practitioners meet you before and after the block to agree on stop signals and to plan follow-up with your regular therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults already in therapy for attachment difficulties who feel that weekly sessions lose momentum and who can take a few days away from daily demands.
modalities.cautions: Intensive formats can stir up a lot quickly, so this is only for people screened as stable enough, with two practitioners trained in attachment and trauma work, clear stop signals and planned aftercare. It is not suitable during a crisis, and it does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Twin Guide Intensive. A few days of planned ideal parent imagery, where one practitioner guides the scenes and a second watches your comfort and calls pauses. For people in therapy who feel weekly sessions lose momentum. Not for a crisis.

modalities.name: Lineage of Kind Hands
modalities.tagline: A whole imagined line of caring people standing behind you.
modalities.whatItIs: Lineage of Kind Hands widens ideal parent imagery, a method built on picturing care from invented ideal parents, from one pair of parents to a whole imagined line of caring people behind them. You picture ideal grandparents and elders who once cared for your ideal parents, so the care you receive has a long, steady history instead of having to be produced by your own effort.
modalities.coreIdea: Care that seems to come from a long line of people, rather than from wishing yourself well, might feel more solid and less fragile to receive.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a trained therapist first guides a familiar scene with ideal parents, then slowly adds the people who raised them, each one passing on a particular kind of warmth. Later sessions imagine the whole line gathered around the child you picture being, and you end by naming one thing from that line you want to carry with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel they come from a long line of hurt, or who feel alone in having to make up for what was missing.
modalities.cautions: Thinking about family lines can bring up painful family history, including real losses or harm across generations, so this needs a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps the imagined lineage clearly separate from the real one. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Imagine being cared for by a whole line of people, not just two. Lineage of Kind Hands is a new idea: a therapist guides imagery of ideal parents and the ideal elders who raised them. For people who feel they come from a long line of hurt. Untested.

modalities.name: They Come Back
modalities.tagline: Imagined goodbyes that always end in a reunion.
modalities.whatItIs: They Come Back is an untested concept built on the part of secure attachment that is about time: trusting that care continues while someone is out of sight. In guided imagery, ideal parents leave for short, clearly explained absences and always return, and the scenes stretch those separations gradually.
modalities.coreIdea: Where insight meditation shows that every experience passes, this practice does the opposite and builds a felt sense that a caring bond lasts through absence and change.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides scenes in which ideal parents say goodbye, explain when they will be back and return on time, starting with a few minutes in the next room and building up to a night away. Each scene ends with the reunion, and between sessions you can listen to a short recording of a return before a separation that worries you, such as a partner's trip.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who panic when someone close is away or slow to reply, or who expect every goodbye to be the last.
modalities.cautions: Scenes of separation can stir up real memories of abandonment, so this is only for work with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care who builds the steps slowly. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments for anxiety or trauma.
modalities.tweet: Experimental concept: They Come Back. Guided imagery where ideal parents leave for short, explained absences and always return, with the gaps growing slowly. For people who panic when someone close is away or slow to reply. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: All Afternoon for You
modalities.tagline: Imagined time with parents who have nowhere else to be.
modalities.whatItIs: All Afternoon for You is a speculative idea that pushes ideal parent imagery toward complete rest and open time, the opposite of anything timed or intense. Each session imagines a long, lazy afternoon in which ideal parents have nowhere else to be, ask nothing of the child you picture being and simply enjoy the time together.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people learned that attention had to be earned or squeezed in, so this practice offers imagined time with no clock, no tasks and nothing to prove.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting or lying comfortably, you follow a therapist's loose, slow guidance into a scene such as a quiet afternoon at home, with fewer set steps than usual and plenty of silence. You are free to let the scene drift, and the session ends with a few minutes of noticing how it feels to have had someone's time without asking for it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who always feel rushed, feel like a burden on other people's time, or believe they must perform to be wanted.
modalities.cautions: Loosely guided imagery can drift toward painful memories or leave some people drowsy or spacey, so the therapist, who should be trained in attachment and trauma work, keeps gently checking in. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: A thought experiment: what if someone had nowhere else to be but with you? All Afternoon for You is guided imagery where ideal parents ask nothing, rush nowhere and simply enjoy your company. For people who feel like a burden on others' time. Untested idea.

modalities.name: Held in Solitude
modalities.tagline: Learning to be alone while still feeling cared for.
modalities.whatItIs: Held in Solitude is an untested concept that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being alone without feeling abandoned. After guided sessions that build a scene of ideal parents, you spend stretches of quiet time by yourself, sensing that the imagined care stays with you even when no one is there.
modalities.coreIdea: A secure child can play happily alone because a caring presence feels close inside, so this practice trains that inner company directly, in solitude rather than with other people.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session begins with a therapist guiding a short scene of ideal parents, then you sit alone in a quiet room for 20 to 40 minutes, with the therapist nearby and a simple way to call them. Afterwards you meet briefly to talk about when the inner company felt near or far, and the alone time grows slowly over the weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find being alone frightening or empty, and who fill every quiet moment with screens, noise or other people.
modalities.cautions: Time alone can bring up loneliness or old fears of abandonment, so the steps must stay small, the therapist (trained in attachment and trauma work) must stay within reach, and anyone at risk of self-harm should not use solitude practice. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For people who find being alone frightening, a new idea: Held in Solitude. A therapist helps you build imagery of ideal parents, then you practice short stretches of quiet time alone, sensing the care stays with you. Untested, built up in small steps.

modalities.name: Little and Often Visits
modalities.tagline: Short, frequent scenes of care instead of long sessions.
modalities.whatItIs: Little and Often Visits proposes delivering ideal parent imagery, the practice of picturing care from invented ideal parents, in very short, frequent sessions instead of long ones. A trained therapist guides brief, tightly structured scenes of about ten minutes, several times a week, so the experience of being cared for comes back often, the way a young child is checked on through the day.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure care is built from many small, reliable moments rather than a few long ones, so in this practice frequency matters more than length or stamina.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three or four times a week you meet a therapist, in person or by video, for a 15-minute slot: a minute to settle, about ten minutes of one scripted scene and a quick check of how you feel. Scenes repeat with small variations, and once a month a longer session reviews how it is going.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find long sessions draining or hard to fit in, or whose sense of being cared for fades quickly between weekly visits.
modalities.cautions: Short slots leave little time to settle if something painful comes up, so the therapist, who should be trained in attachment and trauma work, needs a plan for a longer follow-up when needed. There is no evidence for it yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Little and often, the way a child is checked on all day: the idea behind Little and Often Visits. A therapist guides a ten-minute scene of imagined ideal parents several times a week. For people whose sense of care fades fast. Untested.

modalities.name: Carried for a While
modalities.tagline: Imagery for practicing being helped instead of being strong.
modalities.whatItIs: Carried for a While is an untested concept that uses ideal parent imagery to practice being helped rather than being strong. The scenes picture ideal parents carrying the child, taking the heavy bags, sorting out the problem and letting the child lean on them completely, with no expectation of coping alone.
modalities.coreIdea: People who had to grow up fast may never have felt what it is like to depend on someone, so this practice makes imagined dependence, rather than effort or self-reliance, the main experience.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a trained therapist guides slow, loosely structured scenes of being carried, looked after when ill, or having a grown-up take over a task that was too much. You notice any urge to take back control, let the imagined parents keep carrying, and end by naming one small way you might accept help this week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are always the strong one, find it very hard to ask for help, and feel uneasy when others look after them.
modalities.cautions: Letting yourself lean, even in imagination, can bring up grief about having had to cope alone, so this needs a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For everyone who is always the strong one, an idea: Carried for a While. Guided imagery where ideal parents carry the load and let the child you once were lean on them completely. A way to practice being helped. Untested; needs a trained therapist.

modalities.name: The Imagined Home
modalities.tagline: Designing, then visiting, the calm household you never had.
modalities.whatItIs: The Imagined Home is a proposed extension of ideal parent imagery that builds not only the ideal parents but the whole household they keep: the rooms, the meals, the rules and the daily rhythm. Over many sessions you and a therapist design this home in detail, then spend guided time living ordinary days in it.
modalities.coreIdea: Security grows from a predictable everyday world as much as from single moments of comfort, so this practice gives that world a lasting, structured shape in imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: Early sessions are spent describing the house with the therapist: where the child's room is, what breakfast is like, how disagreements are handled and who is home after school. Later, the therapist guides 20-minute scenes of ordinary moments there, and you return to the same rooms each week so that they become familiar.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who grew up in chaotic or unpredictable homes and who long for a sense of order, routine and belonging.
modalities.cautions: Building an ideal home can highlight what your real home lacked and bring up grief or anger, so this needs a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps the imagined home clearly separate from memories. Nothing is known yet about whether it helps, so it should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: What if you could spend time in a calm, predictable imagined home? The Imagined Home is a new concept: with a therapist you design its rooms, meals and routines, then spend guided time there. For people who grew up in chaos. Untested.

modalities.name: The Asking Hour
modalities.tagline: The questions you never asked as a child, kindly answered.
modalities.whatItIs: The Asking Hour is an untested concept that turns ideal parent imagery into a two-way exchange. In the imagined scene, the child you picture being asks the questions children often carry in silence, such as whether they are too much or why people leave, and the imagined ideal parents answer honestly and kindly.
modalities.coreIdea: Unspoken childhood questions tend to get answered by fear, so this practice gives them a chance to be asked out loud and answered with care.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the imagery, you and a trained therapist choose one question you would have wanted to ask as a child. During a guided scene you ask it, wait and let the imagined parents' answer come, with the therapist stepping in if the answer turns harsh, and afterwards you write the answer down in a sentence or two.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who carry nagging questions about their worth or about relationships, and who like the idea of talking with imagined caregivers, not only receiving from them.
modalities.cautions: Questions like these can lead straight to painful memories, so this belongs with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care who keeps the answers clearly imagined, kind and separate from what really happened. It is untested and should not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Novel idea: The Asking Hour. In guided imagery, the child you once were finally asks the big questions (am I too much? will you stay?) and imagined ideal parents answer kindly. For people still carrying those questions. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: No Need to Talk
modalities.tagline: Being cared for without having to explain or perform.
modalities.whatItIs: No Need to Talk is a new idea that removes the social effort from ideal parent imagery: you never have to explain, report or be good company. The session follows a fixed sequence, and you respond only with small agreed hand signals while imagined ideal parents care for the child you picture being.
modalities.coreIdea: For people who learned that closeness means performing, being cared for without having to speak or please anyone might be a new experience in itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the first meeting you and a trained therapist agree on the script and on three signals, such as one finger for more, two for slow down and an open hand for stop. In later sessions you sit or lie with eyes closed through a 30-minute guided scene, signaling when needed, with only a brief, optional check-in at the end.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel drained by talking about themselves, who people-please in conversation, or who find the social side of therapy exhausting.
modalities.cautions: With little talking the therapist has less to go on, so they need training in attachment and trauma work and must watch closely, and the stop signal must always be honored. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people worn out by talking about themselves: No Need to Talk. A therapist guides imagery of ideal parents caring for the child you once were, and you answer only with hand signals. No explaining, no performing. Untested concept.

modalities.name: Closeness by Degrees
modalities.tagline: Letting imagined care come nearer, one small step at a time.
modalities.whatItIs: Closeness by Degrees is an untested concept for people who find even imagined care too close for comfort. It sets up a step-by-step ladder in which ideal parents start far away, perhaps waving from across a park, and come nearer only as each step feels bearable, until being held feels possible.
modalities.coreIdea: For someone who learned to keep others at a distance, closeness itself may need to be approached in small, planned steps, the way a fear is faced gradually.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained therapist, you write a ladder of about ten imagined scenes, from parents in the distance to parents sitting beside you to a hug, and rate your comfort with each. Each session works on one rung for about 15 minutes, moving up only when your discomfort has dropped and moving back down whenever you need.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who keep people at arm's length, feel smothered by affection, or go blank when someone tries to comfort them.
modalities.cautions: Pushing toward closeness too fast can backfire, so the pace stays in your hands, and the therapist should be trained in attachment and trauma work. There is no evidence for it yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Closeness by Degrees. For people who find even imagined comfort too much, ideal parents start far away and come one step nearer only when you are ready, until a hug feels possible. Untested; done with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Mended Mistake Scenes
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who get it wrong, then make it right.
modalities.whatItIs: Mended Mistake Scenes adds something unusual to ideal parent imagery, a method of picturing care from invented ideal parents: the ideal parents sometimes get things wrong. In planned scenes they are distracted, misunderstand or snap, then notice, apologize and make it right, so the child you picture being learns that a bond can survive mistakes.
modalities.coreIdea: Secure relationships are not perfect ones but ones where breaks get repaired, so this practice rehearses repair rather than flawless care.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist guides structured scenes in three parts: a small, clearly mild misstep by the imagined parents, a pause to notice the hurt, and a warm repair with an apology and a change of course. You rate how safe the relationship feels before and after each repair, and the misstep is always kept small and never resembles real harm.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who experience any conflict or mistake as the end of a relationship, or who cannot forgive themselves or others for small failures.
modalities.cautions: Even mild imagined missteps can echo real hurts, so the scenes must stay small and the work should be done with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma care. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: imagery where ideal parents sometimes get it wrong, then apologize and make it right. Mended Mistake Scenes rehearses repair, not perfection. For people who fear any conflict ends a relationship. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Seen With Kind Eyes
modalities.tagline: The quiet experience of being looked at with delight.
modalities.whatItIs: Seen With Kind Eyes is an untested concept that narrows ideal parent imagery down to one silent experience: being looked at with warmth. There is no music, no story and almost no talking, and the scenes center on an imagined ideal parent's face lighting up as they see the child you picture being.
modalities.coreIdea: Much early attunement happens through faces and eyes rather than through words or sound, so this practice concentrates on the quiet experience of being seen and enjoyed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room, a trained therapist guides a short, structured scene: you picture an ideal parent's face, their eyes finding yours and their expression softening into delight, then you stay with that image in silence for a few minutes. The scene repeats with small variations, such as being seen after a fall or after a success, and ends with a brief check-in.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel invisible, uneasy being looked at, or unsure whether anyone is glad they exist.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at, even in imagination, can feel exposing or stir up memories of cold or angry faces, so this should be done with a therapist trained in attachment and trauma work who keeps it gentle. It has never been tested, so keep any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who feels invisible, an untested concept: Seen With Kind Eyes. Quiet guided imagery of an ideal parent's face lighting up when they see the child you once were. No music, no story, just being looked at with warmth. With a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Thanking the Guards
modalities.tagline: Getting to know your protective habits, and thanking them.
modalities.whatItIs: Thanking the Guards is an untested concept for parts work, which sees the different sides of you as inner characters with their own aims. It works only with protective sides, such as the inner critic, the worrier or the part that keeps you busy, and never goes after the deeper hurts they guard or asks them to change.
modalities.coreIdea: Protective habits may soften when they feel understood and appreciated rather than pushed aside, so appreciation itself is the whole practice, with no imported helpers and no agenda for change.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist trained in parts work, you pick one protective habit, notice it as a side of you, and ask what it is trying to do for you and what it fears would happen if it stopped. You listen, thank it out loud for its effort, and finish without asking it to change, returning to the same protector over several sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel at war with their own habits, such as self-criticism or worry, and who want a gentler way to relate to them before any deeper work.
modalities.cautions: Even friendly attention to protective habits can stir up the feelings they hold back, so this is best done with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work, and people with severe trauma or dissociation should not try it alone. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Thanking the Guards. Sessions spent getting to know the protective sides of you, like the critic or the worrier, and thanking them for trying to help, with no pressure to change. For people at war with their own habits. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Following the Thread
modalities.tagline: No agenda: follow whatever feeling arises, as deep as it goes.
modalities.whatItIs: Following the Thread is a speculative form of parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters, with every plan and goal stripped away. Each session starts with whatever is most alive, a feeling, an image or a body sensation, and simply follows it with the therapist alongside, as far back and as deep as it wants to go.
modalities.coreIdea: Where structured therapies set the agenda, this practice lets the inner world lead, on the idea that it may know its own way and pace better than any plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions run about 75 minutes with no agenda and no homework. You close your eyes, notice what draws your attention, perhaps a tight chest or a young, small feeling, and describe it as it shifts, while a trained therapist tracks you, asks open questions and makes sure each side of you that appears is welcomed rather than pushed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find structured therapy too heady or controlling, and who want room for what lies underneath to surface in its own time.
modalities.cautions: Following inner threads without a plan can lead quickly into very old pain and can blur imagination and memory, so it is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts and trauma work who takes care not to suggest memories. People with dissociation or in crisis need a more structured, stabilizing approach first.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: Following the Thread. No agenda, no worksheet: each session starts with whatever feeling or body sensation is strongest and follows it, with a trained therapist alongside. For people who find structured therapy too heady. Untested.

modalities.name: The Long Witnessing
modalities.tagline: Listening to a hurt part's story for as long as it needs.
modalities.whatItIs: The Long Witnessing is an untested concept that devotes parts work almost entirely to one step: listening to a young, hurt side of you tell its story, for as many sessions as it needs. It does not hurry on to releasing the pain or to present-day goals, because being fully heard is the whole point.
modalities.coreIdea: Hurt sides of us may need to be heard completely, without being hurried toward a solution or a plan, before anything else can change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once your protective sides agree, a trained therapist helps you sit with a young part in imagination and let it show or tell what it went through, at its own pace. You respond with patience and warmth, the therapist keeps checking that you feel calm enough, and each session ends by letting the part know you will come back.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a long-held, old hurt who feel that other approaches moved on too fast or never really listened.
modalities.cautions: Witnessing old hurts can bring up intense trauma memories, and what emerges in imagery is not always an accurate memory, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. People with dissociation or in crisis should start with stabilizing work instead.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea: The Long Witnessing. Parts work devoted to simply listening, for as long as it takes, while the young, hurt side of you tells its story, with no rush to solve anything. For people who feel no one ever really heard it. Therapist-led.

modalities.name: Steady Center Practice
modalities.tagline: Strengthening your calm, curious core instead of chasing problems.
modalities.whatItIs: Steady Center Practice is a proposed form of parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters, that sets symptoms and problems aside and spends each session strengthening the calm, curious state from which the work is usually done. You practice simply being in that steady center, noticing how it feels in the body, and letting any side of you that appears just sit nearby.
modalities.coreIdea: The calm, curious core that parts work relies on may grow steadier with practice, so this practice trains it directly instead of digging for what is wrong.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist trained in parts work guides a few minutes of settling, then asks you to notice moments of calm, curiosity or warmth, where they live in your body and what helps them grow. If a worried or critical side shows up, you simply acknowledge it and invite it to rest beside you, and each session ends with a short practice to repeat at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel they have no stable ground inside, are easily swept up by strong moods, or want a steady base before deeper parts work.
modalities.cautions: Turning inward can still stir up difficult feelings, and some people find calm states unfamiliar or even unsettling at first, so this works best with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: Prototype idea: Steady Center Practice. Instead of chasing problems, each session practices the calm, curious state at your core and lets any anxious or critical side of you sit nearby. For people who feel they have no stable ground inside. Untested.

modalities.name: Round Table of Parts
modalities.tagline: An imagined meeting where every side of you gets a turn.
modalities.whatItIs: Round Table of Parts is an untested concept that brings the sides of you together in one imagined meeting instead of meeting them one at a time. Entirely in words and imagination, with no body work, your calmest self chairs a gathering where the worrier, the critic, the hurt child and others can each speak and hear one another.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner conflicts may ease when every side gets a seat and a turn to speak, the way a family meeting can calm a household.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist helps you imagine a round table and invite the sides of you that are active this week, one by one, checking that each agrees to come. You then let them speak in turn and report what each says, while the therapist helps your calmest self stay in the chair, and the meeting closes with each side saying what it needs next.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults pulled in many directions at once, such as wanting closeness and distance at the same time, who like working with words and imagery.
modalities.cautions: Gathering many sides at once can get crowded and overwhelming, and young, hurt parts should only join when their protectors agree, so this belongs with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. People with dissociative conditions need specialist care rather than this format.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Round Table of Parts. An imagined meeting where the worrier, the critic, the hurt child and the other sides of you each get a seat and a turn to speak, chaired by your calmest self. For anyone pulled in many directions. Therapist-led.

modalities.name: Telling Parts the Year
modalities.tagline: Showing stuck sides of you the life you have now.
modalities.whatItIs: Telling Parts the Year is an untested concept built on a simple observation from parts work: some sides of us act as if we were still small and still trapped in an old situation. Led closely by a therapist, the practice systematically shows these parts the present: your current age, your home, your strengths and the people now in your life.
modalities.coreIdea: A part that still acts as if you were eight years old and powerless may relax once it is shown, clearly and kindly, that time has moved on.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained therapist, you find a side of you that reacts with old panic or helplessness and ask how old it thinks you are. You then show it, in imagination, what your life looks like now, from your adult body to your own front door and the friends you can call, and notice how it responds, repeating the update over several sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose reactions feel much older than their years, such as feeling like a powerless child in arguments or at work.
modalities.cautions: Sides stuck in the past are often linked to painful events, so this should be done with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work who goes at the part's pace. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments for trauma.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Telling Parts the Year. Some sides of you may still act as if you were eight and powerless. This practice shows them, kindly and in detail, the adult life you have now. For reactions that feel far older than you are. Untested, therapist-led.

modalities.name: Parts Atlas Mapping
modalities.tagline: Mapping the sides of you, their jobs and their clashes.
modalities.whatItIs: Parts Atlas Mapping would turn parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters, into careful mapmaking. Over several sessions you and a therapist chart the sides of you on paper, who they are, what jobs they do, which ones protect which and where they clash, so the whole inner system becomes visible at a glance.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing clearly how your inner sides fit together, rather than letting them blur into one open awareness, might make sense of patterns that feel chaotic from the inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session, a trained therapist helps you get to know one or two sides of you, then you add them to a large sheet as circles, with lines for alliances and conflicts and short notes on their fears. Between sessions you mark the map when a part shows up in daily life, and every few weeks you review and redraw it together.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like seeing the big picture, feel confused by their own mixed reactions, or think best with pen and paper.
modalities.cautions: Mapping can feel tidy while stirring up strong feelings underneath, and labeling parts too firmly can make them feel fixed, so it works best with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. It is an untested idea, and people with dissociative conditions need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: Your inner world on one page: Parts Atlas Mapping is a new idea where, with a therapist, you chart the sides of you, like the critic, the pleaser and the hurt kid, with lines for who protects whom. For people confused by their own mixed reactions. Untested.

modalities.name: Protector Job Change
modalities.tagline: Helping a worn-out protective habit choose a lighter new role.
modalities.whatItIs: Protector Job Change is an untested concept that makes one step of parts work its center: helping a protective side of you choose a new role once it no longer needs to guard so hard. It runs as a structured, closely guided process with clear stages, from asking permission to trying out the new job in daily life and reviewing how it went.
modalities.coreIdea: Protective habits rarely vanish, but they might be willing to retrain, so the practice negotiates a deliberate change of role instead of hoping the habit fades on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over a planned series of sessions, a trained therapist guides you to ask a protector what it would rather do if it were free, check that the parts it protects are safe enough, and agree on a trial, such as the inner critic becoming a quality checker that speaks up only once. You track the new role for two weeks, report back, and adjust the agreement with the therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who already know their protective habits well, such as perfectionism, people-pleasing or constant vigilance, and want a concrete way to change how those habits operate.
modalities.cautions: Asking protectors to change too soon can trigger a backlash, so the process moves forward only when they agree, and it should be done with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. There is no evidence for it yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Protector Job Change. Your inner critic may have worked overtime for years. This structured process, done with a trained therapist, helps it choose a new, lighter job and try it for two weeks. For people who know their habits well. Untested.

modalities.name: No Forced Warmth
modalities.tagline: Parts work that starts from honest feelings, not manufactured kindness.
modalities.whatItIs: No Forced Warmth is a new idea for parts work with people who cannot summon kindness toward themselves on demand. Instead of trying to generate compassion, you notice honestly how you feel toward each side of you, including dislike, boredom or disgust, and treat those reactions as further sides to get to know.
modalities.coreIdea: Compassion that is forced may not feel real, so this practice starts from honesty and lets warmth arrive on its own, if and when it does.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist helps you find a side of you and then asks the same question again and again: how do you feel toward it right now. Whatever the answer, the therapist welcomes it, helps you get curious about the side of you that feels it, and only moves closer to the original part once some genuine openness appears.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel fake or worse when told to be kind to themselves, or who find self-compassion practices impossible.
modalities.cautions: Honest dislike of a part can feel uncomfortable and may stir up shame, so this needs a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work who keeps the pace slow. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Can't feel kind toward yourself on demand? New concept: No Forced Warmth. Parts work that starts from honesty: you notice how you really feel toward each side of you, even dislike, and get curious about that too. For people who find self-compassion fake.

modalities.name: Meeting the Emergency Crew
modalities.tagline: Getting to know the urges that take over in a flash.
modalities.whatItIs: Meeting the Emergency Crew is an untested concept that focuses parts work on the sides of you that take over in a flash: the urge to binge, lash out, scroll for hours or shut down. Rather than watching urges come and go without reacting, the practice engages them directly and asks what emergency each one is rushing to put out.
modalities.coreIdea: Impulsive urges often act like an emergency crew rushing to stop unbearable feelings, so understanding the emergency may make room for other ways to respond.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly sessions, a trained therapist helps you recall a recent moment when an urge took over and meet the side of you behind it as a character with a job. You ask what it was protecting you from and what it would need in order to stand down, then agree on one small signal it can give you earlier next time.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel hijacked by sudden urges, such as bingeing, rage, compulsive scrolling or numbing out, and who are tired of fighting them with willpower alone.
modalities.cautions: Urges often guard against intense pain, so getting close to them can stir up strong feelings, and this belongs with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. Anyone using substances heavily, self-harming or at risk of harm should get specialist help first.
modalities.tweet: Your urges might be an emergency crew. Meeting the Emergency Crew is an untested idea: parts work that asks what emergency the urge to binge, rage or scroll for hours is rushing to put out. For people tired of fighting urges with willpower alone.

modalities.name: The Slowest Part Leads
modalities.tagline: Parts work paced by your most cautious side, always.
modalities.whatItIs: The Slowest Part Leads is a speculative approach that makes pacing the heart of parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters: the whole process moves only as fast as your most cautious side allows. Sessions are calm, unhurried and loosely structured, with long pauses and frequent check-ins, and nothing deeper is approached until every wary side agrees.
modalities.coreIdea: Pushing past a frightened side of you may backfire, so the practice takes the slowest part's pace as the right pace, however long that takes, the opposite of training at full intensity.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist begins each session by asking which side of you is most wary today and what it needs in order to feel safe, then does only that, even if it means a whole session of settling. You agree on a signal that means too fast, which ends the step at once, and progress is measured by how safe you feel rather than by how far you get.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who felt overwhelmed or flooded by fast-paced therapy before, or who sense part of them slams on the brakes whenever things get close.
modalities.cautions: Even very slow work can surface old pain, so this needs a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work; the gentle pace is a safety feature, not a promise that nothing hard will come up. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: For anyone who felt flooded by therapy before, a new idea: The Slowest Part Leads. Parts work that moves only as fast as your most cautious side allows, with long pauses and a 'too fast' signal that is always honored. Untested; with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Private Inner Rooms
modalities.tagline: Guided inner work where what you find stays yours.
modalities.whatItIs: Private Inner Rooms is an untested concept that lets you do parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters, without telling anyone what you find. The therapist guides each step of the process, but you keep the content silent and private, sharing only short signals such as done, stuck or calmer.
modalities.coreIdea: Some sides of us may only open up when no one else is listening, so privacy and quiet are the main ingredients rather than conversation.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist gives slow, content-free prompts, such as 'notice a side of you that wants attention' and 'ask what it needs', while you sit quietly with eyes closed and work inwardly. You report only one-word updates, and the session ends with ratings of calm and safety rather than a discussion of what happened inside.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel too ashamed, guarded or private to describe their inner life aloud, or whose inner sides go quiet as soon as someone is listening.
modalities.cautions: Because the therapist cannot hear the content, they rely on your signals and ratings to keep you safe, so honest stuck and stop signals are essential and the therapist should be trained in parts-based trauma work. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: What if you could do deep inner work without saying a word about what you find? Private Inner Rooms is a new concept: a therapist guides each step while you keep the content silent, sharing only 'stuck' or 'calmer'. For people too private to talk.

modalities.name: Resting the Drivers
modalities.tagline: Gentle work with the sides of you that never stop.
modalities.whatItIs: Resting the Drivers is a proposed form of parts work, which sees the sides of you as inner characters, aimed at the ones that never let you stop: the sides that push you to work late, train through pain or keep going when you are exhausted. In calm, guided sessions you get to know these drivers and what they fear rest would bring.
modalities.coreIdea: Relentless pushing is often a protective job with a fear behind it, so the practice explores the fear of stopping instead of adding more willpower or stamina.
modalities.whatYouDo: A trained therapist helps you notice the push to keep going as a side of you and ask how long it has been on duty and what it believes would happen if you rested. Over several sessions you negotiate small, agreed rest periods it can tolerate, and you report back on how it reacted.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who overwork, overtrain or cannot relax, and who feel guilty or anxious whenever they slow down.
modalities.cautions: Easing a driving habit can stir up the feelings it kept at bay, such as emptiness or low mood, so this belongs with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work, and burnout or depression may need medical care too. It is an untested idea and no substitute for well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who can't stop: Resting the Drivers. Calm parts work with the sides of you that push you to work late or train through exhaustion, asking what they fear rest would bring. Untested, with a trained therapist.

modalities.name: Inherited Weather
modalities.tagline: Exploring feelings that seem handed down through your family.
modalities.whatItIs: Inherited Weather is an experimental idea that uses parts work to explore feelings and beliefs that seem to have been handed down rather than learned in your own life, such as a family's fear of scarcity or a habit of silence. The stance is open and allowing: you notice and honor what came down the line without forcing it out.
modalities.coreIdea: Some burdens may feel like weather passed down through a family, and recognizing them as inherited might loosen their grip without anyone having to be blamed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In loosely structured sessions, a trained therapist helps you notice a feeling or belief and gently ask whether it feels like yours or seems to come from someone before you. If it feels inherited, you let yourself sense where it came from and who carried it, without forcing any release, and you may later choose, at your own pace, whether to set it down.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who sense that family history, migration, war or hardship shaped feelings they cannot explain from their own life.
modalities.cautions: Family history can stir up grief, anger or loyalty conflicts, and sensing an inheritance is not evidence of specific past events, so this needs a licensed therapist trained in parts-based and trauma work. It is an untested idea, best kept alongside any care you already receive.
modalities.tweet: Ever carried a fear that doesn't seem to be yours? Inherited Weather is a new idea: parts work that gently explores feelings handed down through a family, like scarcity or silence, without blame or forcing. For people shaped by family history. Untested.

modalities.name: Both Sides Hearing
modalities.tagline: A fair hearing for each side of an inner tug-of-war.
modalities.whatItIs: Both Sides Hearing is an untested concept that focuses parts work on inner tug-of-wars: two sides of you pulling in opposite directions, such as one wanting to leave a relationship and another desperate to stay. Each side gets a full, fair hearing from your calmest self before any decision is made.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner conflicts are often between two protective sides that both mean well, so the work listens to each completely rather than letting the louder one win.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained therapist, you name the two sides and imagine them standing a little apart from you, then hear each in turn: what it wants, what it fears and what it protects. You check how each feels about the other, and sessions end with both sides heard rather than with a forced decision.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults stuck in painful indecision, or swinging back and forth between two choices, habits or feelings.
modalities.cautions: Opposing sides can escalate when one feels sidelined, and stuck decisions can carry real stakes, so this is for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work, and urgent safety decisions should not wait on it. There is no evidence for it yet, so it should not replace well-tested care.
modalities.tweet: Torn between two choices? Concept: Both Sides Hearing. Parts work that gives each side of an inner tug-of-war a full, fair hearing, what it wants and what it fears, before anything is decided. For people stuck in painful indecision. Untested; therapist-led.

modalities.name: Dream Visitors
modalities.tagline: Meeting the figures in your dreams as sides of you.
modalities.whatItIs: Dream Visitors is an untested concept that approaches the figures in your dreams as sides of you worth getting to know, in the spirit of parts work. Instead of decoding dreams by rules, you revisit a dream figure in imagination with a therapist and ask it, with curiosity, what it wants you to know.
modalities.coreIdea: Dreams may bring up sides of you that rarely show themselves while you are awake, so meeting them on their own terms could open a different door to the inner world.
modalities.whatYouDo: You bring a recent dream to an open, loosely structured session, and a trained therapist helps you picture one figure from it and notice how you feel toward it. If it feels safe, you ask the figure what it is doing in your dream and what it needs, and you note any answer without forcing a meaning onto it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with vivid or recurring dreams who are curious about them and comfortable working with imagery.
modalities.cautions: Nightmares and recurring dreams can be tied to trauma, so frightening dream figures should only be approached with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work, and dream images are not evidence of past events. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments for nightmares or sleep problems.
modalities.tweet: What if the people in your dreams were sides of you? Dream Visitors is a proposed practice: with a therapist you revisit a dream figure in imagination and ask, kindly, what it wants you to know. For vivid or recurring dreamers. Untested idea.

modalities.name: Part of Me Drills
modalities.tagline: Quiet training in stepping back from strong feelings.
modalities.whatItIs: Part of Me Drills would turn the core skill of parts work, stepping back from a strong feeling until you can see it as one side of you, into a structured, quiet training program. Sessions are mostly silent inner practice, repeated round after round until the skill becomes reliable.
modalities.coreIdea: Being able to say 'a part of me is furious' rather than 'I am furious' may be a skill that grows with repetition, so the practice drills it before any deeper work.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session, a trained therapist calls up a mild feeling, such as a small irritation, and coaches you to notice it, locate it in the body and step back until you feel some space, timing each round. Over the weeks the practice feelings become a little stronger, and you rate how quickly the space appears.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who get swept away by strong feelings and want a concrete, practiced way to find some distance from them.
modalities.cautions: Practicing with feelings can tip into stronger ones, so this untested idea should start with mild material and be done with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based work. Stepping back should never turn into numbing out, and people prone to dissociation need specialist care rather than distance training.
modalities.tweet: 'I am angry' or 'a part of me is angry'? Part of Me Drills is an untested idea: short, quiet practice rounds with a therapist that train the skill of stepping back from a strong feeling. For people swept away by their emotions.

modalities.name: Setting Down Ceremony
modalities.tagline: A prepared, imagined ritual for letting old pain go.
modalities.whatItIs: Setting Down Ceremony is an untested concept that turns the release step of parts work, where a hurt side of you lets go of old pain, into a carefully planned ceremony. The release happens entirely in imagination, using images of fire, water, wind or light, after weeks of preparation and with a set structure before and after.
modalities.coreIdea: A clearly marked, well-prepared ending may help a release feel real and complete, much as rituals mark big changes in life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over several sessions, a trained therapist helps you check that the hurt side has been fully heard and that every protective side agrees, then you choose together which imagined element will carry the pain away. In the ceremony session, you guide the part to hand over what it carries, picture it dissolving, and invite in a quality it would like instead, followed by planned check-ins over the next weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults already in parts-based therapy who have worked through an old hurt and want a clear, meaningful way to mark letting it go.
modalities.cautions: Ceremonies can create pressure to feel released on schedule, so the date is set only once every side agrees, and it should be done with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. As an untested idea, it should sit alongside well-tested treatments rather than replace them.
modalities.tweet: Speculative concept: Setting Down Ceremony. After weeks of preparation with a therapist, a hurt side of you hands over old pain in an imagined ceremony of fire, water, wind or light. For people in parts work ready to mark letting go. Untested.

modalities.name: Biographies of Parts
modalities.tagline: A written biography for each side of you.
modalities.whatItIs: Biographies of Parts is a proposed practice that gives each side of you a full biography, in the spirit of parts work: when it first appeared, what it went through, how its job changed and what it hopes for. Instead of attending to raw sensation, the practice works through story, building a rich, shared understanding of each side with a therapist.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing a part as a character with a history, rather than as a symptom, may make its behavior understandable and its future open to change.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over a few sessions per part, a trained therapist interviews you about one side of you while you answer from what you sense of it: its age, its first appearance, its biggest moments and its wishes. You write the story up together as a page or two, then read it back to the part in imagination and note how it responds.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who love stories, think in narratives, and want to understand why certain reactions keep showing up.
modalities.cautions: A part's story can touch real painful events, and stories built in therapy are interpretations rather than proof of what happened, so this needs a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work. This untested idea is not suited to people with dissociative conditions, who need specialist care.
modalities.tweet: When did your inner critic first show up, and what has it been through? Biographies of Parts is an untested idea: with a therapist you write a short life story for each side of you. For people who make sense of life through stories.

modalities.name: Sitting With Quiet Parts
modalities.tagline: Slow, quiet work with the numb sides that go unnoticed.
modalities.whatItIs: Sitting With Quiet Parts is an untested concept that turns parts work toward the sides of you that make no noise at all: numbness, flatness, the part that says 'I don't care' or simply goes blank. Rather than expressing big feelings, sessions are quiet and slow, giving these silent sides time to be noticed.
modalities.coreIdea: Numb or shut-down sides often protect in silence and get overlooked, so the practice seeks them out and waits with them patiently.
modalities.whatYouDo: In calm, low-stimulation sessions, a trained therapist helps you notice where things feel blank or far away, treat that blankness as a side of you, and ask, without pressure, what it is holding back. You may sit with it in silence for several minutes, and any response, even a faint shrug, counts as contact.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel numb, flat or cut off from their feelings, and who find expressive therapies too loud.
modalities.cautions: Numbness can be a sign of depression or dissociation and can shield very painful material, so this is only for work with a licensed therapist trained in parts-based trauma work, alongside medical advice if low mood persists. It is untested and does not replace well-tested treatments.
modalities.tweet: Feeling numb rather than overwhelmed? New concept: Sitting With Quiet Parts. Slow, quiet parts work with the sides of you that go blank or say 'I don't care', giving them time to be noticed. For people who find expressive therapies too loud. Untested.

modalities.name: Everyday Experiment Lab
modalities.tagline: Small real-life experiments to test your anxious predictions.
modalities.whatItIs: Everyday Experiment Lab is an untested concept that turns the experimental side of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) into nearly the whole practice, with no imagery and no look back at childhood. You run small, planned experiments in daily life to test what you predict will happen, and a coach acts as a scientific adviser rather than a guide through your inner world.
modalities.coreIdea: Beliefs might shift most when they meet real-world results, so the practice swaps talk about the past for testing predictions out in the world, today.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you pick one prediction, such as 'if I speak up in the meeting, people will think I am stupid', write down how strongly you believe it, design a small test and run it. You record what actually happened, compare it with the prediction, and review the results with the coach in a short session or call every week or two.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with anxious or gloomy predictions who prefer action to talk and like the idea of being their own scientist.
modalities.cautions: Experiments mean facing situations that make you anxious, so steps should be small and chosen by you, and no experiment should put your safety, job or health at real risk. Severe anxiety, depression or suicidal thoughts call for a qualified clinician rather than self-run experiments.
modalities.tweet: Be your own scientist. Everyday Experiment Lab is a new concept: instead of talking about the past, you run small weekly experiments in real life to test your anxious predictions and compare what happened with what you expected. Untested; start small.

modalities.name: Decide and Test
modalities.tagline: A fixed decision procedure, then a real-life trial of the choice.
modalities.whatItIs: Decide and Test is a new, untested idea that applies the structure of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) to being stuck between choices. Rather than exploring the different sides of you that pull each way, it sees you as one decision maker, runs a fixed, time-limited decision procedure and then tests the choice in real life.
modalities.coreIdea: Endless inner debate can keep a problem going, so the practice replaces it with a clear procedure, a deadline and a real-world trial of the decision.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach or therapist, you list the options, write down the facts for and against each, predict how you expect to feel after each choice and set a decision date within a week. You then act on the choice for a fixed trial period, record how it actually goes, and review whether to keep it or switch.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who overthink decisions, seek endless reassurance or stay stuck for months, and who like a clear method.
modalities.cautions: Some decisions, such as leaving a relationship or a job, carry real risks and may need specialist advice, and a procedure cannot settle every question of values. Indecision driven by depression, OCD or severe anxiety calls for a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Stuck between choices for months? An idea: Decide and Test. A fixed, time-limited procedure to weigh the facts and set a decision date, then a real-life trial of the choice to see how it actually feels. For chronic overthinkers. New and untested.

modalities.name: The Belief Ledger
modalities.tagline: A daily ledger of evidence for and against one harsh belief.
modalities.whatItIs: The Belief Ledger is an untested concept that pushes the evidence-weighing of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) to its limit. You pick one harsh belief about yourself, such as 'I am a failure', and keep a daily ledger of evidence for and against it, reviewing the balance with a therapist every week.
modalities.coreIdea: Where some therapies teach you to let thoughts be, this practice takes a belief seriously as a claim and keeps a running, written account of whether the facts support it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each evening you spend ten minutes writing entries in two columns, facts that support the belief and facts that do not, sticking to things a neutral observer could check. In weekly sessions the therapist helps you test whether each entry is a fact or an interpretation, rate how strongly you still believe the claim, and draft a fairer replacement belief to track next.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with a persistent harsh belief about themselves who like writing, tracking and concrete evidence.
modalities.cautions: Searching for evidence can turn into rumination or self-attack for some people, so the therapist should watch for this and shorten or pause the ledger. Severe depression or suicidal thoughts call for prompt professional help rather than self-monitoring.
modalities.tweet: Concept: The Belief Ledger. Pick one harsh belief like 'I'm a failure' and keep a daily ledger of checkable facts for and against it, then review the balance weekly with a therapist. For people who trust evidence over pep talks. Untested.

modalities.name: Change the Cues
modalities.tagline: Redesign the cues and surroundings, and skip the why.
modalities.whatItIs: Change the Cues is an untested concept that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward pure, present-day behavior design and leaves the question of why a habit started completely aside. You map the cues, routines and rewards around one unhelpful habit, then redesign your surroundings and schedule so that the helpful choice becomes the easy one.
modalities.coreIdea: Some habits may change faster by changing their triggers and rewards than by understanding their emotional roots, so the practice makes your surroundings the main thing to redesign.
modalities.whatYouDo: For a week you log each time the habit happens: the time, the place, who was there, the feeling just before and what you got from it. With a coach or therapist you then pick two or three changes, such as moving the phone charger out of the bedroom or setting a cue for a walk after work, try them for two weeks and adjust based on the log.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who want to change one specific habit, such as late-night scrolling, procrastination or snacking under stress, and who prefer practical changes to digging into the past.
modalities.cautions: Some habits, such as heavy drinking, disordered eating or self-harm, carry real risks and need specialist care rather than self-designed changes. If a habit keeps returning despite the changes, it may be meeting a deeper need that is worth exploring with a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Change the Cues. Skip the why. Log the times, places and rewards around one unhelpful habit, then redesign your surroundings so the better choice is the easy one. For people who want practical change without digging into the past.

modalities.name: Peer Evidence Panel
modalities.tagline: A small group that helps you question one heavy belief.
modalities.whatItIs: Peer Evidence Panel is a proposed format that moves the evidence-checking of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) into a small, facilitated group, carried entirely by talk. Each member brings one belief that weighs on them, and the group, guided by a trained facilitator, helps weigh it with questions, examples and other possible explanations.
modalities.coreIdea: Other people can often spot a thinking trap more easily than its owner can, so a supportive panel might make a belief easier to question than working alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of five to seven meet weekly for 90 minutes, and two or three members take a turn each time. The person states a belief and how strongly they hold it, the panel asks questions and offers other explanations, and the person then rates the belief again and chooses one small step to test it.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who find it easier to see through other people's harsh thoughts than their own, and who are comfortable talking in a small group.
modalities.cautions: Group settings can feel exposing, and well-meant challenges can feel like criticism, so the facilitator must keep firm rules of kindness, privacy and the right to pass. People in crisis or with severe social anxiety may need individual support first.
modalities.tweet: What if a small group helped you question your harshest thoughts? Peer Evidence Panel is a new concept: members take turns bringing one belief, and a facilitated panel asks questions and suggests other views. For people kinder to others than to themselves.

modalities.name: Pin the Worry Down
modalities.tagline: Turning vague dread into one precise, testable sentence.
modalities.whatItIs: Pin the Worry Down is an untested concept that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward precise language. Instead of waiting for a vague feeling to become clear in its own time, you and a therapist turn fuzzy dread, such as 'everything is going wrong', into exact, checkable statements that can then be tested.
modalities.coreIdea: Vague worries are hard to answer, so pinning them down in precise words might shrink them to a size that can be examined and acted on.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session you bring one foggy worry, and the therapist asks pointed questions about what exactly, by when, how likely and how bad, until the worry becomes a sentence such as 'I may miss Friday's deadline by a day'. You then plan one concrete test or action for that precise statement and report back the following week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults troubled by a general sense of dread or a feeling that everything is wrong, who like clear thinking and practical steps.
modalities.cautions: Pointed questions can feel pressuring, and not every feeling needs to be argued with, so the therapist must keep a warm, collaborative tone. Persistent dread can also be a sign of anxiety or depression that needs a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Fuzzy dread is hard to answer. Proposal: Pin the Worry Down. A therapist helps you turn 'everything is going wrong' into one precise, checkable sentence, then you test it. For people who feel vaguely doomed and want something concrete. Untested.

modalities.name: Sprint and Scoreboard
modalities.tagline: Two-week sprints toward one goal, with visible daily progress.
modalities.whatItIs: Sprint and Scoreboard is a speculative idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward performance coaching. Instead of letting change unfold in its own time, you work in two-week sprints toward one concrete goal, with a visible scoreboard of small daily actions and a short review at the end of each sprint.
modalities.coreIdea: Clear targets, short deadlines and visible progress may build momentum for people who stall without them.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start of a sprint, you and a coach pick one goal, such as finishing a job application, and break it into daily actions of 15 minutes or less, which go on a scoreboard on paper or in an app. You tick off each action as you go, note what got in the way, and in a 30-minute review you adjust the plan for the next sprint.
