modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel stuck or low in motivation, respond well to deadlines and visible progress, and want help turning intentions into action.
modalities.cautions: Scoreboards can feed perfectionism or self-criticism, so missed days count as information rather than failure, and goals stay small. Low motivation can be a sign of depression, which needs proper assessment and care rather than more pressure.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who stall without deadlines: Sprint and Scoreboard. Two-week sprints toward one goal, broken into 15-minute daily actions you tick off, with a quick review at the end. Untested, and missed days count as information, not failure.

modalities.name: Big Practice Day
modalities.tagline: Weeks of practice packed into one planned day with a group.
modalities.whatItIs: Big Practice Day is an untested concept that packs weeks of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) practice into a single, tightly planned day with a small group. Every hour is scheduled, with short teaching followed by many rounds of practice, such as testing feared predictions or facing feared situations step by step, and trained facilitators support each person.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing many practice rounds in one day, with support close at hand, might build confidence that is hard to gather in short weekly sessions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to eight participants arrive in the morning with a personal plan agreed beforehand, and the day alternates 20-minute teaching blocks with practice rounds, breaks and debriefs until late afternoon. Each person leaves with a written plan for keeping the practice going over the next month, plus a follow-up call.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with anxiety, such as social or performance fears, who struggle to keep momentum in weekly therapy and can set aside a full day.
modalities.cautions: A full day of facing fears is tiring and can feel intense, so participants should be screened beforehand, everyone keeps the right to pause, and the facilitators must be trained clinicians. It is not suitable during a crisis or for severe depression.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Big Practice Day. Weeks of practice packed into one planned day with a small group, many short rounds of facing fears step by step, with trained facilitators close by. For people who lose momentum in weekly sessions. Untested.

modalities.name: Clear No Studio
modalities.tagline: Rehearsing limits and requests until saying no feels possible.
modalities.whatItIs: Clear No Studio is a new idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward plain, firm communication. Where loving-kindness practice quietly wishes everyone well, this practice trains another side of healthy relationships: saying no, setting limits and asking for what you need, rehearsed out loud in a small group.
modalities.coreIdea: Limits may be easier to set once you have rehearsed the words many times in a safe room and tested what you fear will happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly two-hour sessions, a trained facilitator helps four to six members role-play real situations, such as declining extra work or asking a relative to stop a hurtful joke, and members swap roles to try different responses. Before each rehearsal you write down what you fear will happen, then compare it with how the role-play and a real-life try actually went.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who people-please, struggle to say no, or swallow their needs to avoid conflict.
modalities.cautions: Setting limits in real life can have real consequences, and with an abusive or controlling person it can be unsafe, so real-life tries should be chosen carefully with the facilitator. Severe social anxiety may need individual support first.
modalities.tweet: Saying no is a skill. Idea: Clear No Studio. A small group where you rehearse real situations, like turning down extra work or asking someone to stop a hurtful joke, then test your fears in real life. For people-pleasers. Untested; facilitator-led.

modalities.name: Coping Plan Circle
modalities.tagline: Turning each big what-if into a written coping plan.
modalities.whatItIs: Coping Plan Circle is an untested concept that takes worries about the future and turns each one into a concrete coping plan, in the spirit of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy). Rather than watching anxious thoughts come and go, members of a small group spell out their feared scenarios in imagination and write step-by-step plans for what they would do if the worst happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Dread may lose some of its pull when you know exactly what you would do next, so the practice replaces open-ended worry with written plans.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 90-minute sessions, a trained facilitator helps four to six members each pick one what-if, such as losing a job, and imagine it clearly enough to plan around. Members help each other list practical steps, sources of help and first actions, and each person leaves with a one-page plan to keep.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who worry about the future a lot and feel calmer when they have a plan.
modalities.cautions: Imagining feared scenarios can briefly raise anxiety, and planning can turn into endless worry, so each session is time-limited and ends with the plan set aside. Persistent worry that disrupts daily life may be generalized anxiety, which deserves a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Worried about a big what-if? Coping Plan Circle is a proposed group practice: you imagine one feared scenario, like losing your job, clearly enough to write a one-page plan for exactly what you would do. For worriers who feel calmer with a plan. Untested.

modalities.name: Slow Motion Replay
modalities.tagline: Replaying a heated moment frame by frame, in calm.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Motion Replay is an experimental idea that takes the heat out of thought-catching in CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) by doing it in deep calm. After settling into a relaxed state, you replay one recent upsetting moment in imagination, frame by frame, noting the thought, feeling and urge at each step.
modalities.coreIdea: Thoughts that rush past in a heated moment may become visible when the scene is replayed slowly in a calm body, the opposite of working at full intensity.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist guides about ten minutes of slow breathing and relaxation, then helps you replay a scene, such as an argument, pausing every few seconds to name what you were thinking and feeling. Together you mark the frame where things turned, consider what else you could have thought or done there, and rehearse that alternative once in imagination.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults whose reactions happen too fast to catch, such as sudden anger or panic, and who like a calm, methodical approach.
modalities.cautions: Replaying upsetting moments can stir up strong feelings, so choose recent, everyday situations rather than traumatic events, which need trauma-focused care. If the replay becomes overwhelming, stop and return to settling.
modalities.tweet: What if you could replay a heated moment frame by frame, calmly? Slow Motion Replay is a new idea: after relaxing, a therapist helps you slow down a recent argument or panic and spot the exact thought where it turned. For fast reactors. Untested.

modalities.name: Notebook Correspondence
modalities.tagline: Therapy by structured notebook and written replies.
modalities.whatItIs: Notebook Correspondence is an untested concept that runs CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) almost entirely in writing, between you and a therapist. You work alone and quietly in a structured notebook, and the therapist reads your entries and writes back detailed comments and next steps, like a slow conversation by letter.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing alone, at your own pace and with time to think, might help some people do more thoughtful work than they can manage face to face.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you spend two or three short sittings on notebook exercises, such as recording difficult moments, the thoughts behind them and possible alternatives. You send the pages to your therapist, who replies within a few days with written feedback and the next exercise, and you meet by video once a month to review.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who think best in writing, find face-to-face talking hard, or cannot easily attend regular appointments.
modalities.cautions: Written exchanges are slow, so this format is not suitable in a crisis, and you need a clear way to reach urgent help. Notes should be stored and sent securely to protect your privacy.
modalities.tweet: Therapy by notebook? Notebook Correspondence is an untested concept: you work quietly in a structured notebook, your therapist reads it and writes back comments and next steps, like a slow conversation by letter. For people who think best in writing.

modalities.name: Done in the Room
modalities.tagline: All the practice happens live, with no homework at all.
modalities.whatItIs: Done in the Room proposes removing homework from CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) and doing all the practice together with the therapist during sessions. Where most CBT asks you to practice alone between visits, here the therapist leads every exercise live, step by step, so nothing depends on stamina or willpower at home.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people cannot keep up practice alone, so moving all of it into longer guided sessions might make the method usable for them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions last about two hours, once or twice a week, and each one includes a full practice block led by the therapist, such as filling in a thought record together or making a hard phone call while the therapist sits beside you. You leave with no tasks, only a short summary of what you did.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who have dropped out of therapy because of homework, live in chaotic circumstances, or find it hard to get started on their own.
modalities.cautions: Longer sessions can be tiring and costly, and some skills may fade without practice at home, so progress in this untested format should be reviewed regularly. Severe depression or suicidal thoughts call for prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: Hated therapy homework? Concept: Done in the Room. All the practice happens live in longer sessions with your therapist, from thought records to that dreaded phone call, so nothing depends on willpower at home. For people who can't self-start. Untested.

modalities.name: Rulebook Rewrite
modalities.tagline: Finding your unwritten rules and rewriting them as guidelines.
modalities.whatItIs: Rulebook Rewrite is an untested concept that focuses CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) on the unwritten rules you live by, such as 'I must never let anyone down' or 'if I rest, I am lazy'. Rather than pushing yourself harder, you find these demands, trace where you learned them and rewrite them as flexible guidelines.
modalities.coreIdea: Rigid rules can turn ordinary life into a constant test, so loosening them might lighten the load rather than building more strength to carry it.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist, you collect your rules by noticing words like must, should and always in your thoughts, write each one down and test what happens when you bend it slightly. You then draft a gentler version, such as 'I try to keep promises and can say when I cannot', and practice living by it for a few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who are perfectionist, harsh with themselves or worn out by their own standards.
modalities.cautions: Rules often protect against fears, so bending them can bring up anxiety, and changes should be small. If perfectionism comes with disordered eating, severe anxiety or depression, work with a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Living by rules like 'I must never let anyone down'? Rulebook Rewrite is a new idea: find your unwritten rules, test what happens when you bend them, and rewrite them as flexible guidelines. For perfectionists worn out by their own standards. Untested.

modalities.name: Reassurance Fast
modalities.tagline: Gradually cutting back on reassurance to learn to sit with doubt.
modalities.whatItIs: Reassurance Fast is an untested concept that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward coping with uncertainty without outside comfort. Step by step, you cut back on asking others whether things are okay, checking, or searching online for reassurance, and learn to sit with not knowing.
modalities.coreIdea: Reassurance soothes for a moment but can teach you that you cannot cope with doubt on your own, so cutting back gradually might show that the doubt fades by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist or coach you list your reassurance habits, rank them from easiest to hardest to drop, and agree on a first step, such as waiting 30 minutes before asking. You note the urge, what you predicted would happen and what actually happened, and you review progress every week or two while most of the practice happens on your own.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults caught in cycles of seeking reassurance, such as repeatedly checking symptoms online, asking a partner whether they are still loved, or rereading messages.
modalities.cautions: New or worrying physical symptoms still need a doctor, and cutting back on reassurance should never mean skipping proper medical care. Reassurance seeking that is part of OCD or health anxiety is best tackled with a clinician trained in those conditions, and loved ones should agree to the plan.
modalities.tweet: Checking, asking, searching, and the doubt always comes back? An idea: Reassurance Fast. Step by step you cut back on seeking reassurance and learn to sit with not knowing. For people caught in checking loops. Untested, best planned with a therapist.

modalities.name: Ten Other Stories
modalities.tagline: A timed drill for finding other explanations fast.
modalities.whatItIs: Ten Other Stories is a new idea that turns the search for alternative explanations in CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) into a brisk, game-like drill. Given an upsetting situation, such as a friend not replying, you race against a timer to come up with ten other possible explanations before settling on the most likely one.
modalities.coreIdea: Flexible thinking may be a skill that improves with fast, frequent repetitions, much like drills in a sport, so speed and volume are the point.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each session a therapist reads out short everyday scenarios, then one of yours, and you have two minutes per scenario to list ten explanations, however silly. You then rate how likely each one is, notice how your feeling shifts, and practice a few rounds a day at home with a list of scenarios.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who jump to the worst conclusion, such as assuming rejection or blame, and who enjoy quick games and challenges.
modalities.cautions: Timed drills can feel pressuring and are not meant to brush aside real problems, so the therapist should keep it playful and take real concerns seriously. If negative thinking comes with severe depression or suicidal thoughts, get professional help promptly.
modalities.tweet: A friend hasn't replied. Is it really rejection? New concept: Ten Other Stories. A timed, game-like drill where you list ten other explanations before picking the likeliest. For people who jump to the worst conclusion. Untested, best kept playful.

modalities.name: Alone Time Ladder
modalities.tagline: Step-by-step practice at being comfortable on your own.
modalities.whatItIs: Alone Time Ladder is an untested concept that applies the step-by-step approach of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) to the fear of being alone. With a therapist planning and reviewing every step, you practice spending gradually longer periods by yourself, without calls, messages or company, and test what you fear will happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people fill every moment with contact because being alone feels unbearable, so practicing solitude in planned steps might show that it can be survived and even enjoyed.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a therapist you build a ladder from 10 minutes alone at home, with your phone silenced but within reach, up to a full evening or a solo day trip, and write down your prediction for each step. You climb one rung at a time, record what actually happened, and review each step in weekly sessions where the therapist sets the next one.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who feel panicky, empty or unsafe when alone and rely on constant contact to feel okay.
modalities.cautions: This is about tolerating time alone, not about withdrawing from people, and anyone at risk of self-harm should not practice being out of contact. Steps should be small, with a clear plan for reaching someone if distress gets too high.
modalities.tweet: Can't stand being alone? Alone Time Ladder is a new concept: a therapist plans gradually longer stretches of solitude, from 10 minutes with your phone silenced to a solo day out, and you test what you fear. For people who feel panicky alone. Untested.

modalities.name: Finish the Movie
modalities.tagline: Running a feared scene past its worst frame to the end.
modalities.whatItIs: Finish the Movie is a proposed exercise, built on the imagery side of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy), for fears that play like a film frozen at the worst moment. With a therapist guiding every step, you imagine the feared scene and keep it running past its scariest frame, all the way to an ending where the moment is over and life goes on.
modalities.coreIdea: Feared images often stop at the peak of the disaster, so following them through to their end might show the mind that even a bad outcome passes and can be coped with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting indoors with your eyes closed, you describe the feared scene in the present tense, such as freezing during a presentation, and the therapist prompts you to keep going, from what happens next to an hour, a day and a week later. You rate your fear at the frozen frame and at the end, and repeat the movie across sessions until the ending comes easily.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with anxious what-if images that loop, such as embarrassing themselves in public, and who are comfortable working with imagination.
modalities.cautions: This is for everyday fears, not traumatic memories, which need trauma-focused care with a specialist. Imagining feared scenes raises anxiety for a while, so the pace should be set by a trained therapist.
modalities.tweet: Your fear plays like a film frozen at the worst moment. Idea: Finish the Movie. With a therapist, you keep the scene running past the scariest frame to an hour, a day and a week later, when life has moved on. For looping what-ifs. Untested.

modalities.name: Fiction Case Club
modalities.tagline: Practicing thinking skills on invented characters first.
modalities.whatItIs: Fiction Case Club is an untested concept that teaches the thinking skills of CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) through stories about invented characters before turning to your own life. In a small facilitated group, members read short fictional scenes, spot the character's thinking traps and suggest other ways to see the situation.
modalities.coreIdea: It is often easier to see a thinking trap in someone else, even a fictional someone, so practicing on characters might make the skill less threatening to use on yourself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Weekly 90-minute sessions start with a two-page story read aloud, such as a character convinced that a colleague hates them, and the group fills in a thought record for that character. In the second half, each member can link the story to a moment of their own, if they wish, and plan a small step to try that week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who like reading and discussion and who find it hard or exposing to analyze their own thoughts directly.
modalities.cautions: Stories can hit close to home, so members can always pass, and the facilitator should be a trained clinician who checks in with anyone who is upset. People in crisis need individual professional help rather than a group.
modalities.tweet: Easier to spot thinking traps in a story than in yourself? Fiction Case Club is an experimental idea: a small group reads short stories about invented characters, spots their thinking traps and suggests other views, then turns to real life. Untested.

modalities.name: Real Odds Practice
modalities.tagline: Putting honest numbers on your fears.
modalities.whatItIs: Real Odds Practice is a speculative idea that pushes CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) toward plain arithmetic. Instead of expressing fears, you estimate how likely a feared outcome really is, work out the real odds with a therapist, and compare your gut estimate with the numbers.
modalities.coreIdea: Anxiety tends to overestimate both how likely and how bad a feared outcome is, so putting honest numbers on both might bring the fear closer to its actual size.
modalities.whatYouDo: For each fear, such as a plane crash or being fired, you first write your gut estimate as a percentage, then the therapist helps you break it into steps and find realistic figures. You note the gap between gut and numbers, track your estimates for a few weeks, and use the method on your own between sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults with fears that feel far bigger than they probably are, who like logic, numbers and clear reasoning.
modalities.cautions: Some fears are realistic, and numbers do not make a real risk go away, so the method should never be used to dismiss real dangers or medical advice. Fear that persists despite the numbers may need a full assessment by a clinician.
modalities.tweet: Numbers versus dread: Real Odds Practice is a new idea. Write your gut estimate of a feared outcome, then work out the real odds step by step with a therapist and compare. For anxious people who trust numbers more than reassurance. Untested.
